** {{audio|en|en-us-ship.ogg|a=US}}

===Etymology 1===
{{etymon|en|id=vessel|:inh|enm:schip|tree=1}}
{{root|en|ine-pro|*skey-}}
From {{inh|en|enm|chip}}, {{m|enm|schepe}}, {{m|enm|schip}}, {{m|enm|schup}}, {{m|enm|scip}}, {{m|enm|scippe}}, {{m|enm|ship}}, {{m|enm|shup}}, {{m|enm|ssip}}, from {{inh|en|ang|sċip}}, {{m|ang|sċyp}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*skip}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*skipą|t=ship; tub, vessel}}, possibly from {{inh|en|ine-pro|*skey-|t=to split}}. More at {{m|en|shift}}.
{{col-top|2|cog}}
Cognate with {{cog|frr|schap}}, {{m|frr|skap}}, {{m|frr|Skep|t=ship}}, {{cog|stq|Schip}}, {{m|stq|Skip|t=ship}}, {{cog|fy|skip|t=ship}}, {{cog|gmw-cfr|Scheff|t=ship}}, {{cog|nl|schip|t=ship}}, {{cog|de|Schiff|t=ship}}, {{cog|nds|Schipp|t=ship}}, {{cog|lb|Schëff|t=ship}}, {{cog|wym|śejf}}, {{m|wym|siejft|t=ship}}, {{cog|yi|שיף|t=ship}}, {{cog|da|skib|t=ship}}, {{cog|fo,is,nb,nn|skip|t=ship}}, {{cog|sv|skepp|t=ship}}, {{cog|got|𐍃𐌺𐌹𐍀|t=ship}}.
{{col-bottom}}

Compare typologically {{m|en|boat}}, from {{m+|ine-pro|*bʰeyd-}}.

====Alternative forms====
* {{alt|en|shipp|shippe||obsolete}}

====Noun====
[[Image:Amerigo vespucci 1976 nyc aufgetakelt.jpg|thumb|A '''ship''' (senses 1 and 5).]]

{{en-noun}}

# {{senseid|en|Q11446}}{{lb|en|nautical}} A [[water]]-[[borne]] [[vessel]] generally larger than a [[boat]].
#: {{syn|en|keel<q:literary>}}
#: {{hyper|en|watercraft<id:Q1229765>|vessel<id:Q1229765>|<|vessel<id:Q16391167>}}
#: {{hypo|en|merchant ship<id:Q848944>|cargo ship<id:Q105999>|freighter<id:Q105999>|passenger ship<id:subclass of large Q2055880>|;|warship<id:Q2031121>}}
#: {{cot|en|boat<id:Q35872>}}
# {{lb|en|chiefly|in combination}} A vessel which travels through any medium other than across land, such as an [[airship]] or [[spaceship]].
# {{lb|en|cellular automata|chiefly|in combination}} A [[spaceship]].
#* {{quote-newsgroup|en|date=1991-01-10|author=Paul Callahan|title=Questions and comments about Conway's Life (long)|newsgroup=comp.theory.cell-automata|url=https://groups.google.com/g/comp.theory.cell-automata/c/a_UN-cKmHWA/m/fIqysFc-5mkJ|text=I don't know if there is another standard method, but the following approach works: Consider the collision of gliders from three rakes that produces a medium spaceship in the _same_ direction as the rake. This '''ship''' will follow along to the next collision point, which will not produce a spaceship, but rather some stable garbage, consisting of a block and a beehive.}}
# {{lb|en|cellular automata}} A particular [[still life]] consisting of an empty [[cell]] surrounded by six live cells.
# {{lb|en|archaic|nautical|formal}} A sailing vessel with three or more [[square-rigged]] [[masts]].
# A dish or utensil (originally fashioned like the hull of a ship) used to hold [[incense]]. {{defdate|15th century}}
# {{lb|en|cartomancy}} The third card of the [[Lenormand]] deck.
# {{lb|en|dated}} An [[aircraft]].
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1944|author=Wolfgang Langewiesche|title=Stick and Rudder: An Explanation of the Art of Flying
|passage=This means that the landing wheels are not so far forward of the '''ship''''s center of gravity ; and that means that ground contact is less likely to produce a bounce.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1994|title=American Aviation Historical Society Journal|page=107
|passage=In addition to the four NAA pilots, three Air Force and one RAF pilot, all based at Edwards, flew the '''ship''' after first being checked out on the "tether rig."}}

=====Usage notes=====
* The singular form {{m|en||ship}} is sometimes used without any [[Appendix:Glossary#article|article]], producing such sentences as "In all, we spent three weeks aboard ship." and "Abandon ship!". (Similar patterns may be seen with many place nouns, such as {{m|en|camp}}, {{m|en|home}}, {{m|en|work}}, and {{m|en|school}}, but the details vary between them.)
* Ships were traditionally regarded as ladies, especially by the sailor, and the pronouns {{m|en|her}} and {{m|en|she}} are still sometimes used instead of {{m|en|it}}, though this usage is in decline.

===Etymology 2===
{{ety|en|id=to send}}
From {{inh|en|enm|schippen}}, {{m|enm|schipen}}, from {{inh|en|ang|sċipian}}, from {{inh|en|gmw-pro|*skipōn}}, from {{inh|en|gem-pro|*skipōną}}, from {{der|en|gem-pro|*skipą|t=ship}}. {{dbt|en|equip}}.

====Verb====
{{en-verb}}

# {{lb|en|transitive}} To send by [[water-borne]] [[transport]].
#* {{RQ:Knolles Turkes|chapter=The Life of [[w:Suleiman the Magnificent|Solyman]], the Fourth and Most Magnificent Emperour of the Turkes|page=670|passage=All the timber whereof, was {{...}} '''ſhipped''' in the bay of {{smallcaps|Attalia}}{{nb...}}, from whence it was by ſea tranſported to {{smallcaps|Pelusium}}.}}
#* {{RQ:Economist|date=2014-06-14|volume=411|issue=8891|title=[http://www.economist.com/news/science-and-technology/21604091-it-possible-sniff-out-problems-sewer-pipes-they-happen-its-gas It's a gas]
|passage=One of the hidden glories of Victorian engineering is proper drains. Isolating a city’s effluent and '''shipping''' it away in underground sewers has probably saved more lives than any medical procedure except vaccination.}}
# {{senseid|en|verb-send}} {{lb|en|transitive}} To send (a parcel or container) to a [[recipient]] (by any means of transport).
#: {{ux|en|to '''ship''' freight by railroad}}
# {{lb|en|ergative}} To [[release]] (a product, not necessarily physical) to [[vendor]]s or [[customer]]s; to [[launch]].
#: {{ux|en|Our next issue '''ships''' early next year.}}
#: {{ux|en|It [[compile]]s? '''Ship''' it!}}
# {{lb|en|ergative}} To [[engage]] to [[serve]] on board a vessel.
#: {{ux|en|to '''ship''' seamen}}
#: {{ux|en|I '''shipped''' on a man-of-war.}}
#* {{RQ:Melville Moby-Dick|[[s:Moby-Dick (1851) US edition/Chapter 19|chapter 19]]|text=With finger pointed and eye levelled at the Pequod, the beggar-like stranger stood a moment, as if in a troubled reverie; then starting a little, turned and said:—“Ye’ve '''shipped''', have ye? Names down on the papers? Well, well, what’s signed, is signed; and what’s to be, will be;{{...}}}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive}} To [[embark]] on a ship.
#* {{RQ:R. F. Burton Arabian Nights|night=563|text=I '''shipped''' with them and becoming friends, we set forth on our venture, in health and safety; and sailed with a fair wind, till we came to a city called Madínat-al-Sín; {{...}}}}
# {{lb|en|transitive|nautical}} To put or secure in its place.
#: {{ux|en|to '''ship''' the tiller or rudder}}
#* {{quote-journal|en|year=1846|author=editorial staff|title=[[c:File:Scientific_American_-_Series_1_-_Volume_002_-_Issue_13.pdf|Maudslay's Improvements in propelling Machinery]]|journal=Scientific American|section=series 1, Volume 2, Issue 13, page 100
|passage=To the upper part of the frame a chain is attached, and if the screw shaft be drawn back out of the boss, the square frame may be hove up by carrying the chain to a winch—the sliding block maintaining the frame in the perpendicular position. By the use of this contrivance, therefore, the screw may be '''shipped''' or unshipped with facility.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To take in or take on (water) over the sides of a vessel.
#* {{RQ:Maturin Melmoth|I||159|She was half in the water, a mere hulk, her rigging torn to shreds, her main mast cut away, and every sea she '''shipped''', Melmoth could hear distinctly the dying cries of those who were swept away, or perhaps of those whose mind and body, alike exhausted, relaxed their benumbed hold of hope and life together,—knew that the next shriek that was uttered must be their own and their last.}}
#* {{RQ:Haggard She|passage=But as things were it was manageable enough, and we did not '''ship''' a cupful of water.}}
#: {{ux|en|We were '''shipping''' so much water I was sure we would capsize.}}
# {{lb|en|colloquial|with [[dummy it|dummy ''it'']]}} To [[leave]], [[depart]], [[scram]].
#* '''2008 November 21''', Graham Linehan, ''{{w|The IT Crowd}}'', Season 3, Episode 1:
# {{lb|en|ditransitive|colloquial}} To [[pass]] (from one person to another).
#: {{ux|en|Can you '''ship''' me the ketchup?}}
#* {{quote-journal|en|date=September 18, 2011|author=Ben Dirs|work=BBC Sport|title=[http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/rugby_union/14959055.stm Rugby World Cup 2011: England 41-10 Georgia]
|passage=And when scrum-half Ben Youngs, who had a poor game, was burgled by opposite number Irakli Abuseridze and the ball '''shipped''' down the line to Irakli Machkhaneli, it looked like Georgia had scored a try of their own, but the winger's foot was in touch.}}
# {{lb|en|ambitransitive|poker slang}} To go [[all in]].
# {{lb|en|transitive|sports}} To [[trade]] or send (a player) to another team.
#: {{ux|en|Twins '''ship''' Delmon Young to Tigers.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive|rugby}} To [[draw]] (a [[penalty]]) by [[bungle|bungling]] a [[kick]] and giving the [[opposing]] team [[possession]].
#* {{quote-journal|en|date=October 1, 2011|author=Tom Fordyce|work=BBC Sport|title=[http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/rugby_union/15124512.stm Rugby World Cup 2011: England 16-12 Scotland]
|passage=England were '''shipping''' penalties at an alarming rate - five in the first 15 minutes alone - and with Wilkinson missing three long-distance pots of his own in the first 20 minutes, the alarm bells began to ring for Martin Johnson's men.}}
#* {{quote-journal|en|date=February 11, 2015
|passage=They '''shipped''' penalties, lost field position, and in the second-half, having retreated to the changing room buoyed by Dougie Fife’s well-worked try, found themselves ceding two-thirds of the territory and with it, the lion’s share of the ball.|title=Six Nations: Scotland raw but capable of improving|newspaper=The Scotsman}}
# {{lb|en|sports}} To [[concede]](points/goals)
